summary: A 1971 note by R. T. Braden on CCN as a Network Service Center, about the Computer Center at UCLA offering services to the network.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 90 describes UCLA's Campus Computing Network and services it planned to offer to other network hosts. It covers the computer, software, remote job service, interactive systems and planned network protocols.

subtitle: A description of UCLA's planned computing services for ARPANET hosts.

tldr.problem: Other network hosts need information about the hardware, software and services available from UCLA's Campus Computing Network.
tldr.mechanism: R. T. Braden describes CCN's IBM 360/91, its software and storage, and planned remote job, interactive and network services.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a dated service description that distinguishes existing facilities from services still planned for the network.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 90 as Unknown and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC describes CCN's equipment and the services it planned to provide to network hosts as of January 1971.

sections.title: The Campus Computing Network
sections.content:
UCLA's Campus Computing Network (CCN) was preparing to connect to the ARPA Network as a service-center host. The RFC describes its IBM 360/91 Model 91 CPU, fast memory, channels, disk and tape units, consoles and remote terminal interfaces.

The note gives a CPU speed range of 2-6 MIPS, while warning that speed depends strongly on the program.
sections.plainLanguage: CCN planned to offer computing resources to other network sites. The document describes its main computer and the equipment connected to it.

sections.title: Software and Remote Job Services
sections.content:
The RFC lists compilers and other software available at CCN, along with interactive systems such as URSA, APL and OLMS. It says TSO was expected to become available sometime during 1971.

The Remote Job Service lets users submit OS/360 jobs from remote batch terminals; the jobs run in turn and their printed or punched output returns to the originating terminal unless it is rerouted. QUICKRUN is described as a fast batch subsystem for small, simple jobs and is available through RJS as well as a CCN card reader.
sections.plainLanguage: Other sites could send batch jobs to CCN and receive output. The RFC also lists interactive systems and a faster subsystem for small jobs, while marking some services as planned rather than available.

sections.title: Storage, Charges and Network Services
sections.content:
CCN provides online disk space for source programs, object and load modules, and temporary storage. The note says storage and batch use are charged, with batch charges based on CPU time, input/output requests and core-memory region size.

The network service section says CCN plans RJS, URSA and eventually TSO, each with a third-level protocol. NETRJS is described as specified in RFC 88 with implementation targeted for March 1971; NETCRT and NETTYPE are planned, while NETTRANS has not yet been specified.
sections.plainLanguage: The document explains the main kinds of storage and how charges are calculated. It also lists network services and distinguishes protocols that are planned or specified from one that has not yet been specified.

sections.title: A Snapshot of Planned Services
sections.content:
RFC 90 describes CCN's facilities and planned services as of 25 January 1971. Its wording distinguishes current equipment and software from systems and network services that were expected in the future.

The document invites requests and comments from other sites.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a snapshot of what CCN had and what it planned to offer at the time. The author invites other sites to respond with requests and comments.

references.text: NETRJS protocol, specified in RFC 88; implementation targeted for March 1971.
